description: Wing history states Echo shutdown at 0845 on 16 Mar 1967: all 10 LFs lost strategic alert nearly simultaneously; 'normal controlled shutdown'; faults VRSA ch.9 (G&C No-Go) and ch.12 (Logic Coupler No-Go).
provenance: SRC002 (RR0 transcription of 341 SMW history Apr-Jun 1967, p.33ff)

description: Same wing history: 'external generated signals' judged possible by the investigation team but 'very remote'; only identified mechanism was coupler self-test command + partial reset; further study referred to contractor.

Wing history records power fluctuation at E-1 at 1453 on 16 Mar 1967, commercial power restored 1921; Fergus Electric attributed it to transformer short at Winifred substation. Also a similar Alpha Flight shutdown on 19 Dec 1966 with same capsule crew and weather/power failure.

Wing history says UFO rumors for Echo were 'disproven' and a Mobile Strike Team checking November Flight LFs reported nothing unusual — conflicts with testimony that crews saw UFOs near Echo LFs; interview sourcing of that statement undocumented.
provenance: SRC002 p.37 (citing Engineering Investigation Report p.27)

description: Klotz & Salas (1996) place Salas at November Flight on 16 Mar 1967 (4-5 missiles faulted), whereas the book (2008) places Salas at Oscar Flight on 'probably March 24' with 6-8 missiles — an internal inconsistency in the testimony chronology.

Hastings states the engineering report was 'never made available' and Salas says AF told Boeing/Ogden team head not to write a final report; but the wing history cites an Engineering Investigation Team report dated 23 Mar 1967 (which exists, classified Secret) and says contractor follow-up study was planned.
Kingston George (SI 1993): film debrief and secrecy cautions occurred; film later destroyed; supports existence of a classified filming and of a debrief, differs on interpretation and date (22 Sep).

Launch lists show Atlas D 245D ABRES LORV-3 RV test on 15 Sep 1964 15:27 UTC (08:27 PDT) as a PARTIAL FAILURE (manual cutoff after SECO); book cites 'Atlas D 245H'. A launch malfunction is an untested alternative explanation for a warhead falling short.

Time discrepancy: book (from EA) gives 22 Sep 1964 NTMP KX-19 launch at 13:08 GMT; Wikipedia list gives 15:27 UTC for 22 Sep (identical to 15 Sep) — likely data error; sunrise vs launch-time consistency (George says pre-dawn) not resolved.
Official contemporaneous wording for Loring 27 Oct 1975: 'unidentified helicopter' (TWZ, secondary) / 'A/C' penetration (NMCC teletype quoted by NICAP); Hastings and NICAP treat it as UFO incursion.

FBI 31 Jan 1949 memo exists (3 pp, San Antonio office to Director); describes Top Secret treatment of 'Flying Discs' and Los Alamos concentration; also, per ufopedia, FBI Asst Dir Ladd recommended Bureau decline Army requests because many reports were pranks — context omitted by the book.
Halt memo dating error acknowledged by both book and Wikipedia: first event ~0300 on 26 Dec 1980 (memo says 27 Dec); lighthouse and fireball explanations cited by sceptics.

Chadwell memo quotations appear verbatim in a curated excerpt page; CIA Reading Room text not obtained; a CIA release dated 9 Dec 1952 and Deputies' meeting notes (12 Dec) show DCI Smith was not satisfied with the memo (search summary only).

Quintanilla's 13 Nov 1968 statement is verbatim in the Tulien report; it ALSO states 'The physical violation of the lock of OSCAR 7 does not seem to be related to UFOs'. The book's summary of the Minot case omits the Oscar-7 intrusion.

Base Ops dispatcher entries: 'LATER SIGHTINGS OF BRIGHT LIGHTS AND FLASHING GREEN AND WHITE LIGHTS ACCOMPANIED BY A LOW JET ENGINE SOUND CORRELATES WITH THE B-52 MAKING A VOR PENETRATION, LOW APPROACH AND MISSED APPROACH' (Col. Werlich comment, per Tulien). Supports a conventional-aircraft explanation for part of the ground sightings; book does not mention it.
RAPCON line: 'Somebody is seeing flying saucers again' (Tulien transcript) vs book 'Someone is seeing flying saucers again' — minor quotation variance.
Arithmetic: two miles in one 3-second sweep = 2,400 mph, not 3,900 mph; Tulien states the 3,900 mph figure came from the 14-frame sequence. The book's stated derivation is internally inconsistent.

Florida Today column text (Gross copy) matches the book on Nelson (Site 9, 'guards were scared', could not leave post), Caplan (dimmed lights, OSI interrogation) and Lamb (did not see anything). Column notes three Atlas silos were destroyed by fuel explosions at Walker, a stressful context. Hastings dates the column June 2001; copy index says Oct 2001 — date unresolved.

Atlas deployment facts: Wikipedia lists 579th SMS at Walker AFB (12 Atlas F, 30 Nov 1962-5 Jan 1965) — consistent with book; but states first operational Atlas squadron went on alert at F.E. Warren in Sept 1959 with 6 Atlas D; Warren total 15 (6+9) and Offutt 9 match book; the book's '31 Oct 1959 at Vandenberg' and '6 at Vandenberg' do not match this source.

Condon Report comparison: Wikipedia confirms quoted Low memo text and committee members (incl. Hartmann, Wertheimer, Levine); report 965 pp paperback/1,485 hardcover; also notes consultant Rothberg 'about 100 cases, three or four puzzling' and critics that enigmatic cases were 'buried'. Book's '91 sightings' and 'nearly 30%' not confirmed here.

Frazier: Wikipedia says he worked full-time at Sandia 1983-2006 writing about its research and editing the Sandia Lab News for the last 11 years; consistent with book's 'two decades'; Wikipedia biography itself discloses Sandia, though the SI masthead may not.
Hastings' Ch13 argues the identity/affiliation of skeptics undermines their conclusions (genetic/ad hominem reasoning). It contains no new incident evidence; its value is argumentative.

Werlich's Memo for the Record (24 Oct 1968), quoted by Shough: 'Initially the target traveled approximately 2½ mile in 3 sec or at about 3,000 mi/hr' (arithmetic: 2.5 mi/3 s = 3,000 mph). His 29 Oct telex instead says an echo closed from 3 mi to ~1 mi off the left wing, with no speed. The Blue Book file therefore has TWO different official speed statements; neither is '2 miles in 3 s = 3,900 mph'.
provenance: SRC023 (quoting Blue Book file); verification of original memo pending

description: Origin of '3,900': Shough reconstructs it as the simple average of two rates computed from echo displacements relative to the B-52 between frames 771-772 and 772-773, using antenna paint-time-corrected intervals (3.8 s and 1.3 s): ~1,990 kt and ~5,870 kt, co-altitude upper limits, mean ~3,900 KNOTS (~4,450 statute mph). Hence Clark's number is knots, a mean of very unequal rates, an upper limit, and not '2 miles per sweep'.

Analyst recomputation (this project): from Shough's measured echo positions (771: 138 deg/1.62 NM; 772: 242 deg/1.05 NM; 773: 40 deg/1.05 NM; azimuth from nose, slant range) the displacements are 2.13 and 2.06 NM. With a naive 3.0 s per frame: ~2,560 and ~2,470 kt (~2,950/2,850 mph) relative speed. With Shough's paint-time intervals (3.8, 1.3 s): ~2,020 kt and ~5,710 kt (matches Shough ~1,990/5,870 within ~3%); their simple mean is ~3,865 kt (reproducing '3,900'), but the time-weighted mean over the 5.1 s is only ~2,960 kt (~3,400 mph). Script: database/build/analysis/minot_speed.py.
provenance: Derived from SRC023 numerical values; not independent measurement of the photographs

description: Assumptions behind any speed figure: (i) the three echoes are one target (Shough: cannot be justified from two possibly unrelated echoes; elongated echoes are suggestive but not conclusive); (ii) co-altitude (a depression angle lowers true separation; e.g. at 50 deg the naive horizontal speed would be ~1,650 kt, ~1,900 mph); (iii) range scale inferred (~5 NM display, no indicator on photographs); (iv) only 14 of probably >100 frames survive. The result is an upper-limit estimate, not a measurement of a 3,900 mph object.

[SUPERSEDED by EVD034] Timeline dispute between analysts: Shough concludes frames 771-783 were taken late in the event near the missed approach (so the 'fast' echo transit is not the start); Poher concludes the radarscope clock (0906Z) runs ~9 min ahead of the approach-controller clock so frames coincide with radio loss at ~0858 COM when the B-52 was ~21 nm out (early). The question of when the high-speed transit occurred relative to ground sightings is unresolved in the sources I read.

[PARTLY SUPERSEDED by EVD040] Dispatcher log vs B-52 explanation: entries 0828-0830Z mention jet engines; the B-52 low approach/missed approach was ~0904-0917 COM (Poher). So the Blue Book statement that 'later sightings ... correlate with' the B-52 low approach is plausible for entries after ~0900Z but not demonstrated for the 0800-0858Z entries; and entries 0940-1010Z (after the log says the B-52 landed at 0940Z) describe a stationary object west of N-7 on/near the ground, which the B-52 cannot explain.

Analyst astronomical check (this project; simple GMST/precession, Minot AFB 48.42N 101.36W, 24 Oct 1968): Sirius altitude 11-23 deg, azimuth 132-162 deg (SE to SSE) from 0800Z to 1010Z; Vega 7 deg->-2 deg altitude, azimuth 325-348 deg (NW-NNW), setting ~0940Z. Dispatcher entries 0800Z 'S/E of N-7' fit Sirius direction; entries 0940-1010Z 'west of N-7' do not (~110 deg off); Blue Book cites Vega at azimuth 345 at 0435 local (matches my 342 deg) but the pilot's light was 'west-northwest' (~50 deg away) - requires check of the AF Forms 117. Script: database/build/analysis/minot_sirius.py.
provenance: Computed; positions accurate to ~0.5 deg; atmospheric refraction ignored

description: Blue Book's own text (SRC025) says no data were submitted for the possible 0335 local air visual and 0352 weather-radar paint, and that the pilot's Form 117 puts his sighting at ~0435 local, not 0335: official file acknowledges data gaps in the timeline; Hastings' narrative does not.

Transcript time base: COM clock is Zulu (landing 0940Z matches dispatcher log and pilot's request to 'touch down at 40 past'; CDT = Z-5 with DST still in effect on 24 Oct 1968). All earlier 'local time' mismatches in the file are 1-hr/20-min inconsistencies in individual witness entries, not in the transcript.

Transcript 0852: controller says weather radar also sees the object at the B-52's 1:00, 3 miles; B-52 replies 'We have nothing on our airborne radar and I'm in some pretty thick haze'. Omitted from the book's narrative, which says RAPCON was told weather radar tracked the object 'near Bowbells, ND, 38 nm NW' (Bowbells does not appear in the transcript).

Pilot radio reports (transcript 0902/0904): echo at ~1.25-1.5 mi left of the aircraft from 'about the time we left 200 to about 14 [thousand]' and 'till about 10'; radio trouble began 'exactly' then. Together with the ~10-11.5 k ft altitude derived from the photos, this places frames 771-783 in the latter part of the echo episode (about 0858-0902Z), 3-5 min after first report near FL200.

CORRECTION to EVD027: the Shough/Poher 'early vs late' contrast is narrower than I first reported. Both altitude models put the frames at ~10-11.5 k ft MSL, i.e., late in the echo episode and after the FL200 turn; they differ mainly on clock offset (Shough 7-8 min with caveats; Poher 9 min; my linear-descent estimate 5-6 min). The fast transit in frames 771-773 is therefore not the 'initial' fast approach described by Werlich/McCaslin. See documents/minot_1968_timeline.md.

Partin's Form 117 (30 Oct 1968) describes a stationary 'bright orange ball of light' ~15 mi away at 1 o'clock on/just above the ground, 'miniature sun placed on the ground'; it does not mention an oblong shape, windows, or a tubular section. Those details appear in later interviews quoted by the book (Partin: 'oblong ... windows'; Runyon: barn-sized with a tube, 32 yrs later). The form's sketch shows a small circle with 'a very dim ring of soft white light'.

Partin's reported time (0430-0435 CDT = 0930-0935Z) does not match the transcript (downwind leg 0910Z = 0410 CDT; final 0928Z); the file's annotation 'should be 0335 CDT' (an hour earlier) matches neither. Blue Book used 0435 for its Vega calculation.

Vega test of the Blue Book 'air visual' explanation (analyst calculation): bearing OK — Partin's 1 o'clock from heading 290 magnetic is ~328-332 deg true (declination 8-12 E) vs Vega az 336-337 deg at 0906-0910Z. Brightness FAILS — Vega was only ~1.4 deg->0.4 deg high (airmass 23-33): extinction ~4.6-6.9 mag at 0906Z (k 0.2-0.3), so Vega would appear ~mag 5-7 or fainter, not a 'bright orange ball'/'miniature sun'. Also the light 'remained stationary as we flew toward it' and the aircraft passed ~1 mi south of it, which a star cannot do. A terrestrial light (e.g., ground light, other aircraft) or misjudged range is more consistent than Vega.
provenance: Computed; positions ~0.5 deg; extinction coefficients assumed

description: Ground-observer forms: Smith — reddish burnt orange, twinkling like a star, slight green, on the horizon, ~15 deg elevation, no edges (compass mark appears S-SW; Sirius was SE-SSE: low-res reading, needs checking); O'Connor — white ball -> dim green -> dim amber, facing south, final mark ESE-SE at ~20 deg (matches Sirius direction/elevation) and a Blue Book annotation 'Characteristic colors of Sirius'; Isley — lights 'like head lights or landing lights' on the front and a green flashing light toward the middle or rear, shape/size not determinable, two objects at one time (more aircraft-like); Bond — point of light with fuzzy edges ~10 mi from N-7, two objects, second seen ~3 min, Mohall town lights 4 mi. The observers' descriptions are not uniform: some fit a scintillating Sirius, one suggests an aircraft.

Internal conflict in the file: transcript 0913Z says missile-site personnel 'don't see anything anymore'; dispatcher entries 0940-1010Z say N-7 still sees an object 3 mi west, stationary near the ground. Different sites/time bases are not established.

CORRECTION to EVD028: the transcript shows the B-52 was in the Minot area around 0828-0834Z ('TA calibration check to rw 11', climbing out on heading 290 at 0834), so the 0828-0830Z 'jet engines heard' entries may well be the B-52 — partly supporting the Blue Book aircraft explanation for the earliest entries. The post-0940Z entries (object W of N-7 after the B-52 landed) remain unexplained by it.
